lines: A doctor ties a tight cord around a man's bare arm.
He is William Harvey, a London physician.
Doctors trust the ancient writer Galen.
Galen taught that the liver keeps making fresh blood.
Harvey does the math, keeping every number low on purpose.
Each heartbeat pushes out about a sixth of an ounce of blood.
The heart beats 1,000 times every half hour.
In one day, the liver would need to make 498 pounds of blood.
That is more than a whole body weighs.
You see, it's like a fountain in a town square. It doesn't make new water. The same water goes round and round.
So Harvey ties off the veins of snakes and fish. Their hearts go empty.
He ties the arteries. The hearts swell up.
On the man's arm, Harvey finds little bumps in the veins. They are valves.
Blood pushed toward the heart moves easily. Pushed the other way, it will not move.
Blood travels in a circle.
In 1628, Harvey publishes his book in Frankfurt.
Other physicians attack it.
So many patients leave that his practice falls mightily.
Slowly, his idea wins anyway.
Harvey lives to see his circle accepted, yet dies unsure of what he achieved.

claims.claim: A physician tied a tight ligature onto the upper arm of a person; below it the arm was cool and pale.
Harvey was an English physician who established himself in London.
Galen's accepted view held the liver as the origin of venous blood; scientists studied the writings of Galen and it was almost an impiety to question them.

Harvey's estimates were purposefully low: about 1/6 fluid ounce per beat, 1,000 beats every half hour, so the liver would have to produce 498 pounds of blood a day, more than the weight of the whole body.
Tying the veins of serpents and fish emptied the heart; tying the arteries made it swell.
Harvey noticed little bumps in the veins, the valves; blood pushed down the arm would not move but moved easily up toward the heart, so blood travels in a circle.
In 1628 he published De Motu Cordis in Frankfurt; after negative comments by other physicians he 'fell mightily in his practice'.
His ideas met vociferous opposition but eventually triumphed; he lived to see his theory gain wide currency and died uncertain of his achievement.
